summary: Describes authentication mechanisms for the IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE command, which identifies a user to the server and can negotiate protection for later traffic. The mechanisms covered include Kerberos, GSSAPI and S/KEY.

plainLanguage.summary: IMAP4 has a command called AUTHENTICATE that a mail client uses to prove who it is before it can open a mailbox. This RFC defines three ways to do that: Kerberos version 4, GSSAPI, and S/Key. Two of them also let the two sides agree how to protect the session that follows.

questions: how does kerberos work with imap
subtitle: Three ways an IMAP4 client can prove who it is, and how each one can protect the rest of the session.

tldr.problem: An IMAP4 server has to know who is connecting before it lets a client read or change a mailbox, and the two sides often need a way to protect what they say afterwards.
tldr.mechanism: The AUTHENTICATE command runs a challenge and response exchange in which the mechanism decides what the server challenges with and what the client answers. Kerberos version 4 and GSSAPI both finish by agreeing a bit-mask that names how the rest of the session is protected.
tldr.outcome: The three mechanisms defined here, Kerberos version 4, GSSAPI and S/Key, remain the ones the memo specifies for the IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE command, and the RFC is still on the Standards Track with nothing obsoleting it.

today:
RFC 1731 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the document that defines these three mechanisms for the IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE command.

The memo says that security issues are discussed throughout it, and it names the three systems it builds on: Kerberos version 4, the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface described in RFC 1508, and S/Key.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet Message Access Protocol, Version 4 (IMAP4) contains the AUTHENTICATE command, for identifying and authenticating a user to an IMAP4 server and for optionally negotiating a protection mechanism for subsequent protocol interactions. RFC 1731 defines three authentication mechanisms for use with that command: Kerberos version 4, GSSAPI and S/Key.

All three follow the same overall shape, shown in the examples in this memo. The client sends an AUTHENTICATE command naming the mechanism it wants, the server answers with a ready response, the client answers in turn, and the server closes the exchange with a tagged OK or NO. The tag used in the examples is A001, so the last line is either A001 OK Kerberos V4 authentication successful or A001 NO Kerberos V4 authentication failed.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a mail client can read a mailbox, it has to tell the server who it is. IMAP4 does that with a command called AUTHENTICATE. The client names the method it wants to use, the server sends a challenge, the client answers it, and the server says whether it accepts the answer. This RFC describes three methods.

sections.title: Kerberos Version 4 Authentication
sections.content:
The mechanism is named KERBEROS_V4. The data in the first ready response contains a random 32-bit number in network byte order. The client answers with a Kerberos ticket and an authenticator for the principal imap.hostname@realm, where hostname is the first component of the server's host name with all letters in lower case, and realm is the server's Kerberos realm. The encrypted checksum field inside the authenticator carries the server's 32-bit number.

After decrypting and verifying the ticket and the authenticator, the server checks that the checksum inside equals the number it sent. If the check passes, the server adds one to the checksum and constructs 8 octets: the incremented checksum in the first four octets, a bit-mask naming the protection mechanisms the server supports in the fifth octet, and the maximum cipher-text buffer size the server can receive in the sixth through eighth octets. The server encrypts those 8 octets with the session key and issues them in a second ready response.

The client treats the server as authenticated when the first four octets of the decrypted data equal one plus the checksum it sent. The client then constructs its own data: the original checksum in the first four octets, the bit-mask of the protection mechanism it selected in the fifth, the maximum cipher-text buffer size it can receive in the sixth through eighth, and the user name string after that. It appends one to eight octets so the data length is a multiple of eight octets, encrypts the result with the session key using PCBC, and sends it. The server decrypts the data, verifies the checksum, and verifies that the principal in the Kerberos ticket is authorised to connect as that user name. After both verifications the authentication is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The server starts by sending a random number. The client answers with a ticket from Kerberos that carries the same number inside it, so the server can tell that the answer is fresh and meant for it. The two sides then agree a protection setting and each send an encrypted block, one of which also carries the name of the user the client wants to act as.

sections.title: GSSAPI Authentication
sections.content:
Every mechanism built on the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSSAPI) shares the authentication type GSSAPI. The server's first ready response contains no data. The client calls GSS_Init_sec_context with a target name built from the string SERVICE:imap@hostname, where hostname is the fully qualified host name of the server with all letters in lower case, and answers with the resulting output token. If the call returns GSS_CONTINUE_NEEDED, the client expects a token from the server in a later ready response and passes it to another call. If it returns GSS_COMPLETE, the client answers with any remaining output token, or with no data, and then waits for the server's final token.

The client passes the server's last token to GSS_Unseal. The first octet of the resulting cleartext is a bit-mask naming the protection mechanisms the server supports, and the second through fourth octets are the maximum size message the server can receive. The client constructs data with the bit-mask of the protection mechanism it selected in the first octet, the maximum size message it can receive in the second through fourth octets, and the user name string after that. It passes the data to GSS_Seal with the confidentiality flag set to FALSE and answers with the generated message. The client can then consider the server authenticated.

On the server side, the first ready response carries no data, and the client's token is passed to GSS_Accept_sec_context as the input token, with the acceptor credential handle set to NULL to use the default credentials. When that call returns GSS_COMPLETE, the server constructs 4 octets: the protection bit-mask in the first octet and the maximum size token it can receive in the second through fourth octets. It seals the plaintext with the confidentiality flag set to FALSE and issues the result in a ready response. It then unseals the client's token, reads the selected bit-mask, the maximum message size and the user name, and checks that the source name is authorised to authenticate as that user name.
sections.plainLanguage: GSSAPI hands the whole exchange to a security library rather than defining its own steps. The client and the server pass tokens back and forth through that library until it reports the exchange is complete. Each side then reads the protection setting and the maximum message size out of the final token, and the client sends the user name inside a sealed block.

sections.title: S/Key Authentication
sections.content:
The mechanism is named SKEY. The server's first ready response contains no data, and the client responds with the user name string. The data in the second ready response contains the decimal sequence number followed by a single space and the seed string for the indicated user. The client responds with the one-time password, either as a 64-bit value in network byte order or encoded in the "six English words" format. Once the one-time password has been verified, the server considers the client authenticated.

S/Key authentication does not provide for any protection mechanism, so the IMAP4 session that follows it is unprotected.
sections.plainLanguage: S/Key is the simplest of the three. The client sends the user name, the server sends a seed and a sequence number, and the client answers with a one-time password derived from them. Each password works only once, and it protects nothing after the login: the rest of the session runs in the clear.

sections.title: Protection Mechanism Bit-Masks
sections.content:
Two of the three mechanisms also settle how the rest of the session is protected. The choice travels as a bit-mask, a single octet in which each value names one protection mechanism.

  • Value 1: no protection mechanism.
  • Value 2: integrity protection. Kerberos version 4 calls this krb_mk_safe, and GSSAPI describes it as the sender calling GSS_Seal with the confidentiality flag set to FALSE.
  • Value 4: privacy protection. Kerberos version 4 calls this krb_mk_priv, and GSSAPI describes it as the sender calling GSS_Seal with the confidentiality flag set to TRUE.

The client sends the bit-mask of the mechanism it selected, and the server reads that choice back out of the sealed message. Each side also states the largest cipher-text buffer it can receive, so neither peer sends more than the other can take.
sections.plainLanguage: After the login succeeds, the two sides can still choose how much protection the session gets. The choice is a one-byte code: no protection, protection that detects changes, or protection that also hides the content. S/Key offers none of these.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says security issues are discussed throughout it, and the sections above show where each decision is taken. The Kerberos version 4 and GSSAPI mechanisms both verify a ticket or a token before the user is accepted, and both check the principal or source name against the user name the client supplied, so a client cannot ask to act as a user its credentials do not cover.

The S/Key mechanism proves only that the client holds a valid one-time password. It provides no protection mechanism, so the IMAP4 commands that follow are sent unprotected.
sections.plainLanguage: Each mechanism decides something different about safety. Kerberos and GSSAPI check that the client is entitled to use the user name it asked for. S/Key checks only a one-time password and leaves the rest of the session unprotected.
